lesson.title: How Fast Does It Repeat? Measuring Frequency
lesson.summary: Frequency counts how many times a periodic waveform repeats each second, and it is the direct reciprocal of the period you already know how to read off a scope trace.
lesson.body:
Every periodic signal, whether it is the 60 Hz hum from a wall outlet or the megahertz clock inside a microcontroller, has two ways of describing how fast it changes. One is the period, the time it takes to complete one full cycle, measured in seconds. The other is frequency, the number of complete cycles that happen in one second, measured in hertz (Hz). These two quantities are reciprocals of each other: f = 1/T. If you already know how to find the period of a waveform by reading the distance between two matching points on an oscilloscope trace, finding the frequency is just a matter of flipping that number over.

Why bother with two names for essentially the same information? Because each one is more natural in a different context. Period is the quantity you actually measure directly on an oscilloscope, since the horizontal axis is time. Frequency is the quantity engineers design around, since filters, radios, and audio equipment are specified in hertz, not seconds. A 20 kHz low pass filter is a far more useful label than a filter with a 50 microsecond period cutoff, even though the two describe related ideas. Keeping the reciprocal relationship in mind lets you move fluidly between a time domain measurement and a frequency domain specification.

Worked example: suppose you connect an oscilloscope to the AC output of a European wall socket and measure the time between two consecutive rising zero crossings of the sine wave, finding it to be 20 milliseconds, or 0.02 seconds. That is the period, T = 0.02 s. The frequency is simply f = 1/T = 1/0.02 = 50 Hz. This matches the standard mains frequency used across most of Europe, Asia, and Africa, so the measurement checks out against a real, known value. If you repeated the measurement in North America, you would expect T to be about 16.67 milliseconds, giving f = 1/0.01667, approximately 60 Hz, the standard mains frequency there.

Frequency also tells you something physical about repetition rate that period, expressed in seconds, tends to hide because the numbers get awkwardly small. A 1 MHz signal has a period of only one microsecond, and writing 0.000001 seconds is both error prone and hard to reason about compared to simply saying one megahertz. This is part of why almost every datasheet, radio dial, and audio specification is written in hertz, kilohertz, megahertz, or gigahertz rather than in periods measured in fractions of a second.

One common mistake is confusing the number of times a signal changes state with the number of complete cycles. A single cycle of a sine wave includes one full rise and one full fall back to the starting point, so counting only the peaks, or only the zero crossings in one direction, gives you the cycle count directly. Miscounting half cycles as full cycles is a frequent source of a factor of two error, so always confirm you are measuring from one point back to the same point on the next repeat of the identical shape, not just any similar looking feature.
